theme: Finding God's love after betrayal, loneliness, or lost faith—and the extraordinary joy of heaven when one soul begins to return to Him.
opening: Can a heart wounded by betrayal, loneliness, or disappointment find its way to God again? What if a single moment of wondering about His love could become the beginning of an extraordinary transformation? Explore the mystery of repentance, the lost sheep, and why Jesus says heaven rejoices when one soul returns.
prayer: Heavenly Father,  How extraordinary it is to know that heaven rejoices when even one of Your children turns toward You.  Thank You for loving us with a love greater than our understanding, for seeking us when we wander, and for never ceasing to invite us into communion with You.  Today I pray especially for those who have left the Church, those who have been wounded by others, and those who believe they have wandered too far to return.  May they come to know You as You truly are, not through the imperfections of man, but through the love and mercy of Your Son.  Help me to be an instrument of that love. May my words, my actions, and these reflections reach someone who needs to know that they are not forgotten.  And Lord, when we approach Your altar, open our hearts to the wonder of what we are receiving. Never let us become so accustomed to Your presence that we forget the extraordinary gift of communion with You.  May we find You, our peace, our refuge, and our eternal home.  And having found You, may we remain close to You all the days of our lives.  Amen.
body:
"In just the same way, I tell you, there will be rejoicing among the angels of God over one sinner who repents.”*


Can you imagine the rejoicing in heaven when just one person turns toward God?

I try to imagine it. The glory, the joy, the celebration among the angels over one soul who has found its way back to the Father. Not because that person has accomplished something extraordinary in the eyes of the world, but because someone who was lost has been found.

One person. That is all Jesus speaks of.

There is something so beautiful about knowing that heaven rejoices over us. That our return to God is not met with reluctance, disappointment, or a reminder of how far we have wandered, but with joy.

I sometimes feel I have witnessed a small glimpse of that heavenly celebration during Mass.

Every Easter, when I watch those entering the Catholic Church approach the altar to receive the Eucharist for the first time, I am overcome with a feeling I find difficult to describe. There is something extraordinary about watching someone come into communion with Christ. I wonder whether the joy I feel is just a small reflection of what takes place in heaven.

And I experience that same feeling during an ordinary Mass, as we prepare to receive the Body and Blood of Christ.

I look around and see people rising from their pews, quietly making their way toward the altar. Each person carrying a life I know little or nothing about. Their struggles, their hopes, their sorrows, their gratitude. And yet we are all approaching the same table, seeking the same Lord.

Sometimes I watch the priest as he looks upon the people coming forward. There is something moving about seeing a shepherd welcoming the flock entrusted to his care.

It feels transcendent.

This is no ordinary banquet. We are approaching Christ Himself, who desires to give Himself to us.

And I wonder whether we sometimes become so accustomed to these moments that we forget how extraordinary they really are.

Today's first reading also reminds me of St. Paul, who identifies himself as a descendant of the tribe of Benjamin. I had not realized that about him before.

Here was a man who once persecuted Christians, believing he was defending God. Yet through his encounter with Jesus, his entire life changed. The man who had worked to destroy the Church became one of its greatest builders.

What an irony. What a conversion. And what a beautiful example of God's ability to reach someone who has lost his way, even someone who doesn't realize he is lost.

I have read many of these passages before, as I imagine most of us who attend church have. But when I slow down and really absorb each word, I discover something greater than I understood the last time.

Scripture is so much bigger than you or me. There is always something more to discover about the depth of God's love.

And I keep returning to the lost sheep.

How fortunate would we be to help someone find their way back to Christ?

I think about those who have left the Church. Those who have been hurt, disappointed, confused, or discouraged. Those who have come to associate God with the failures of the people who claimed to represent Him. And those who have simply drifted away, perhaps without even realizing how far they have gone.

I wish I could tell each one of them that God has not forgotten them.

That is part of why I write these reflections.

I want these reflections to find you.

You who have wandered away. You who have never really known Jesus. You who once believed but now wonder whether there is a place for you with Him. And you who are still growing in faith, trying to understand Him a little more each day.

I want you to know how deeply our loving Father desires communion with you.

If your experience with human beings has left you questioning God, I encourage you to look beyond those experiences and discover who He really is. You do not have to pretend that your wounds never happened. But please do not let the failures of others be the final word on the love God has for you.

Come to know Jesus for yourself.

He wants to embrace you, encourage you, help carry your burdens, and lead you toward a love unlike anything we can fully experience through another human being.

A love that is patient with our weakness, yet strong enough to transform us. A love that calls us toward truth without abandoning us in our struggles.

A transcendent love.

And when we turn toward Him, heaven rejoices.

What moves me most is that Jesus does not describe the lost sheep as an inconvenience to the shepherd. He describes a shepherd who searches until he finds it, lifts it onto his shoulders, and carries it home rejoicing.

There is no suggestion that the sheep must first prove itself worthy of being found.

It is precious because it belongs to the shepherd.

And perhaps that is what I hope we all come to understand: we are precious to God before we have figured everything out, before we have overcome every weakness, and even when we have wandered farther than we ever intended.

Our return matters to Him.

So today I pray for those who have forgotten Him, those who have not yet discovered Him, and those of us who are still learning how to love Him more completely.

May we recognize the extraordinary invitation that stands before us.

May we find in Jesus the peace we have been searching for.

And having found Him, may we never willingly walk away from that love again.

Because somewhere beyond what our eyes can see, heaven rejoices when even one of us comes home.

And that one could be you.
title: Rejoice with Me
